feedback.end: A cake would not taste very nice if cooking was a reversible change, and the cake turned back into its individual ingredients when cooled.

atoms.b: Some changes to substances are irreversible. Ingredients being baked into a cake is an example of ((++an_irreversible a_reversible)) change.

instruction.text: Put the log on the fire.

atoms.a: What will happen to the log?
b: It will stay as it is.

atoms.a: The fire is extinguished safely after a few hours. Will the log look the same as it did before it was burnt?
b: ++No, the log will have become a new material: ash.
Yes, the log will look exactly the same.

feedback.finish: This kind of irreversible change is very useful as we need electricity to carry out most of our daily activities.

atoms.b: Burning is an example of ((++an_irreversible a_reversible)) change.
Burning fuels, such as wood, coal and gas, produces heat energy, which can be used to produce ((++electricity water)).

instruction.text: Ella has shaped some clay to make a mug. Put the mug into the kiln.

atoms.a: What will happen to the clay?
b: ++The heat will dry out and harden the clay.

atoms.a: Ella waits for the mug to cool down and then she uses it to make a coffee. What will happen to the mug?
b: The mug will get wet and soften as it mixes with the coffee.

feedback.end: This is a very useful irreversible change. Mugs would become useless if they could become wet clay again.

Watch what happens when bicarbonate of soda is mixed with vinegar.

atoms.a: What could have been produced to cause this?

feedback.correct: Bicarbonate of soda reacts with vinegar to produce the gas carbon dioxide.

atoms.a: What else shows that a gas was produced?

text: Once this reaction takes place, it is not possible to separate the mixture.
